source.title: Pearl Harbor — the day and the year after (LUSORA script, video vid_4d5de5a2e04d)

notes:
L1, and read the level before reading the numbers. There is no reference video behind this case: it is a script LUSORA itself wrote, and the marks are a judgement about where a graphic belongs in it, not a measurement of what a real channel did. They were written from script.txt WITHOUT opening the beats.json they are scored against, which is what makes the baseline honest rather than circular — but a self-marked case can only tell you whether the planner agrees with one reading of a script, and it cannot tell you whether that reading is what a professional editor would do. Replace it with an L2/L3 teardown case as soon as one exists (docs/10-overlay-marks.md).

The budget is the whole point here. doc-slow is density 'normal' = 2.5/min, and the narration runs about a minute, so roughly four overlays are legal in total — against thirteen spans that carry a real anchor. Nine of the marks below are therefore negatives on legal anchors: the question this case asks is not 'can the planner find a number' but 'can it spend four graphics on the right four'.

marks.why: a real date anchor in the first six words, and the reflex is a DateStamp on it. With four overlays for the whole video, spending one on the premise rather than on the toll, the quote or the vote is the wrong trade — the date is what the viewer is told, not what they are asked to hold.
precision the script never uses again. Nothing later in the narration refers back to the minute, so a graphic here buys nothing and costs one of four.

the strongest of the negatives, and the closest call in the case. It is a genuinely good figure — and it sits one sentence before three more, and the one that lands is the last of them. A counter here means a second counter within about eight seconds, which is the stacking the density budget exists to prevent.

marks.source_words: eight battleships had been sunk or damaged
marks.why: first of three figures in a single breath. Putting a card on each turns one sentence into a slideshow, and none of the three is read.
second of the same three. Same reason as m4.
the third of the three, and the one the sentence is built to land on. The other two are scale; this one is the cost. If the video carries exactly one number, it is this one.

a name anchor, and a NamePlate on it is decoration: the audience for this script does not need Roosevelt identified. A name card earns its place when the viewer would otherwise not know who is speaking.

the shape this moment wants is the draft itself, with the struck phrase visibly replaced by the new one. DocumentCard shows a document and HighlightedPassage marks a passage in set type; neither strikes text out and neither animates an edit. No field carries it, so the moment is excluded rather than scored as a miss the planner had no way to avoid.

marks.source_words: a date which will live in infamy
marks.why: a quote anchor, and the most quoted sentence of the century. The script spends four sentences setting up an edit to one phrase; the phrase has to be on screen or the setup was spent on nothing. HighlightedPassage would be the other reading, but this channel's pack does not allow it.
two quantities set against each other, and the asymmetry IS the fact — a split reads it instantly in a way the spoken number does not.

the discriminating negative of the pair. It is exactly as legal as m10 and it is the second vote in two sentences: a viewer who has just read one lopsided split reads the next as a repeat, and two cards for one point halve each other. Choose one; the Senate's is first and rounder.
the setup half of a comparison whose payoff is the next clause. Graphing the two halves separately breaks one comparison into two weak counters — the ratio is the fact, not either number.
the payoff, and the closing image of the script. A split carrying both years is the better read because the point is the multiple; a counter on 1,900 alone is defensible and loses the comparison.
